title: Graphics, Photographs and Video
bigQuestion: How did people who skate turn boards, pictures, films and music into an art world of their own?

story.title: Forty Years on a Shop Wall
story.kicker: A row of old decks in a small skate shop reads like a history book with pictures.
paragraphs: On a Tuesday afternoon a woman in her fifties walks into a neighborhood skate shop to buy wheels for her nephew. Above the counter, the owner has screwed about thirty old decks to the wall in a long row. The first one is a narrow plank of plain wood with no picture at all. The last one is wide, with a curved nose and tail and a bright painted scene across the bottom.

She stops in the middle of the row. A deck with a cartoon hand screaming in pain catches her eye, then one covered in skulls and swords. "I remember these," she says. "My brother had that one taped to his bedroom wall. He never rode it. He said it was too nice to scratch." The owner laughs and tells her that plenty of people did the same thing in the 1980s.

Next to the decks hang a few things that are not boards. There is a faded magazine cover from the 1980s, a hand-stapled photocopied booklet with smudged pictures, and a VHS tape case with a skeleton on it. Under them, a small screen plays a skate clip on a loop with a fast punk song behind it.

The owner points at the row. "People think skating is just tricks," he says. "But look. Somebody drew these. Somebody shot these photos and cut these videos together. Somebody picked the music." The woman takes a picture of the wall with her phone before she leaves with the wheels.
story.think: Why might someone keep a skateboard on the wall instead of riding it, and what does that tell you about how people saw the art on it?

lessons.title: From Plain Planks to Painted Decks
lessons.mainIdea: Early decks were mostly plain, and graphics grew into a major art form once companies, teams and pro models gave artists a reason to draw.
reading: The first store-made skateboards, sold around 1959 and through the early 1960s, looked a lot like small surfboards. Many were plain wood, sometimes painted one color, with a company name stamped or printed on top. Their job was to be ridden and sold, not to be looked at. A *deck graphic* is the art printed on a skateboard deck, usually on the bottom, and in those years there was very little of it.

That changed in the 1970s and especially the 1980s. Companies built teams of sponsored skaters, and each top skater could get a *pro model*, a deck sold with that skater's name and their own graphic. A skater's board became a kind of flag. Young riders bought the deck of the skater they admired, so the picture on the bottom had to be strong enough to be seen across a skatepark or in a magazine photo.

The bottom of the deck became the canvas for a practical reason. The top is covered with *grip tape*, a sandpaper-like sheet that keeps shoes from slipping, so art there disappears. The bottom shows when a skater flies out of a ramp, flips the board or carries it. The bottom also gets scraped by rails, ledges and curbs, so every graphic slowly wears away. Many skaters see that wear as part of the board's story.

words.d: the art printed on a skateboard deck, usually on the bottom
a deck sold under a professional skater's name, with that skater's own graphic
a rough, sandpaper-like sheet stuck to the top of the deck so shoes do not slip

look.title: Two Decks Side by Side
look.text: Picture two boards on a table. The first is from the early 1960s: narrow, flat, plain wood, with a small printed name near the front. The second is from the late 1980s: wider, with a kicked-up tail, and its whole bottom is covered in a bold drawing in three or four colors. Turn both over. The top of the first is bare wood. The top of the second is covered in black grip tape.
look.prompt: Which deck was made to be seen, and what clues on the board tell you that?

check.q: Why do most deck graphics go on the bottom of the board?
choices: The top is covered with grip tape, so art there is hidden
Paint does not stick to the top of maple
Rules at contests ban art on the top
check.why: Grip tape covers the top so shoes do not slip, so the bottom is where art can be seen.

check.q: What is a pro model deck?
choices: A deck used only at the Olympics
A deck sold under a professional skater's name with their own graphic
A deck with no graphic at all
A deck made of plastic instead of wood
check.why: A pro model carries a sponsored skater's name and graphic, and fans bought it to support that skater.

check.q: What did most store-made boards around 1959 and the early 1960s look like?
choices: Wide decks with full-color art on the bottom
Mostly plain wood, sometimes one color, with a small company name
check.why: Early boards were mostly plain; detailed graphics grew in the 1970s and 1980s.

lessons.title: Jim Phillips at Santa Cruz
lessons.mainIdea: Jim Phillips, an artist for Santa Cruz, drew bold cartoon graphics such as the Screaming Hand that became some of the best-known images in skating.
reading: Jim Phillips was an artist from Santa Cruz, California, who drew for surf culture before he drew for skateboards. He became the main graphic artist for Santa Cruz, a skateboard company, from the 1970s into the 1990s. His style used thick black outlines, bright flat colors and wild cartoon energy. You can recognize it from across a room.

His most famous image is the *Screaming Hand*, a blue hand with an open, yelling mouth in its palm. It first appeared in the mid-1980s and has been printed on decks, shirts, stickers and wheels ever since. A graphic that a company uses again and again, until people know the company from the picture alone, works like a *logo*. The Screaming Hand became exactly that for Santa Cruz.

Phillips also designed graphics for individual pro models, matching each picture to a skater's name or personality. His work shows that deck art was not decoration added at the end. It was planned art made for a long, narrow shape with rounded ends, a hard space to fill well. Later artists studied how he used that shape, placing the main image so it still read clearly when the board was moving.

words.d: a California artist who drew graphics for the Santa Cruz skateboard company, including the Screaming Hand
Jim Phillips's image of a blue hand with a yelling mouth in its palm, first used in the mid-1980s
an image a company uses again and again so people recognize the company from it

look.title: Filling a Long, Narrow Space
look.text: Imagine you are handed a blank deck and a pencil. The space is about four times as long as it is wide, with rounded ends that curve up. A square drawing would leave big empty bands at the nose and tail. A drawing that runs the full length, with the strongest shape near the middle, fills it and still shows when the board is upside down in the air.
look.prompt: Sketch or describe how you would fit one bold image onto a deck so it reads from far away.

check.q: Which company did Jim Phillips draw graphics for?
check.why: Jim Phillips was the main graphic artist for Santa Cruz from the 1970s into the 1990s.

check.q: What does the Screaming Hand show?
choices: A blue hand with a yelling mouth in its palm
A skull with a sword through it
A dragon wrapped around a board
A wave breaking on a beach
check.why: The Screaming Hand is a blue hand with an open, yelling mouth in the palm.

check.q: Why does the Screaming Hand work like a logo?
choices: People came to recognize Santa Cruz from the picture alone
It contains the company's phone number
It is hidden under the grip tape
check.why: A logo is an image used again and again until people know the company from it, which is what happened.

lessons.title: Vernon Courtland Johnson and the Skulls
lessons.mainIdea: Vernon Courtland Johnson drew Powell Peralta's skulls, skeletons and the Bones Brigade images that defined how 1980s skating looked.
reading: Powell Peralta was a California skateboard company started by George Powell and Stacy Peralta in the late 1970s. Its team, the *Bones Brigade*, included young skaters such as Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, Lance Mountain, Mike McGill and Rodney Mullen. The company needed a look as strong as the team, and the artist who gave it one was Vernon Courtland Johnson, often called VCJ.

Johnson drew detailed skulls, skeletons, snakes and dragons in pen and ink, full of fine lines and shading. His skull-and-sword design became a symbol of the company and the team. He also drew pro model graphics fitted to each rider, such as a dragon for Steve Caballero and a hawk-like skull for Tony Hawk. The images looked a little dangerous, which fit the way skating felt to many teenagers in the 1980s.

Johnson's graphics did more than sell boards. They tied together the decks, the team, the magazine ads and the company's videos into one recognizable world. Placing Jim Phillips's bold cartoons next to Johnson's fine-lined skulls shows two very different answers to the same problem. Both artists made a narrow wooden board into something people wanted to keep, frame and remember decades later.

words.d: the artist, often called VCJ, who drew Powell Peralta's skulls, skeletons and team graphics
the Powell Peralta skate team of the 1980s, including Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero and Rodney Mullen
a California skateboard company started by George Powell and Stacy Peralta

look.title: Two Styles, One Problem
look.text: Put a Jim Phillips deck beside a Vernon Courtland Johnson deck. The Phillips board has thick black outlines, a few bright flat colors and a big cartoon shape. The Johnson board has a skull drawn with hundreds of fine pen lines and careful shading, almost like an old engraving. Step back three meters. Now step close.
look.prompt: Which style do you think reads better from far away, and which rewards a close look? Explain why.

check.q: Who drew the skull-and-sword design for Powell Peralta?
check.why: Vernon Courtland Johnson, often called VCJ, drew Powell Peralta's skulls and the skull-and-sword.

check.q: What was the Bones Brigade?
choices: Powell Peralta's skate team in the 1980s
check.why: The Bones Brigade was Powell Peralta's team, with skaters such as Tony Hawk and Steve Caballero.

check.q: How did Johnson's style differ from Jim Phillips's style?
choices: Johnson used fine pen lines and shading; Phillips used thick outlines and flat colors
Johnson used no drawings, only words
Johnson drew only waves and palm trees
There was no difference at all
check.why: Johnson's pen-and-ink detail contrasts with Phillips's bold cartoon outlines and flat colors.

lessons.title: SkateBoarder and the Dogtown Stories
lessons.mainIdea: SkateBoarder magazine spread skating's look across the country, and its 1970s Dogtown articles and photos made the Zephyr skaters famous.
reading: A magazine called The Quarterly Skateboarder first appeared in 1964, during the first boom. It soon became SkateBoarder. When the boom faded around 1965 and 1966, the magazine stopped. It came back in the mid-1970s, after urethane wheels brought skating back to life, and for the rest of the decade it was the main way most skaters outside California saw what was happening.

In the mid-1970s SkateBoarder ran a series of articles and photos about the Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice, California, an area some locals called *Dogtown*. Craig Stecyk wrote and photographed many of them, and Glen E. Friedman, a teenager at the time, took photos of the same skaters. Their pictures showed Tony Alva, Jay Adams, Peggy Oki, Stacy Peralta and others riding low and aggressive, like surfers on concrete.

These were not posed portraits. They were *action photography*: pictures taken in the middle of a move, often in empty backyard swimming pools during the 1976 to 1977 drought. A reader in another state could study a photo and copy a skater's crouch, arm position and line. In 2001 Stacy Peralta made Dogtown and Z-Boys, a documentary film that retold this story using many of those photos.

words.d: a nickname some locals used for parts of Santa Monica and Venice, California, home of the Zephyr team
photos taken in the middle of a move rather than posed
a skateboard magazine that began in 1964 as The Quarterly Skateboarder and returned in the mid-1970s

look.title: Reading an Action Photo
look.text: Picture a black-and-white photo from the 1970s. A skater is near the top of the curved wall of an empty backyard pool. Their knees are deeply bent, one hand reaches down toward the concrete, and their eyes look ahead at the next part of the wall. Behind them is a wooden fence and a palm tree. No one is smiling at the camera.
look.prompt: What could a skater in another state learn about technique from this single photo?

check.q: When did The Quarterly Skateboarder first appear?
check.why: The Quarterly Skateboarder first appeared in 1964, during the first boom.

check.q: Who wrote and photographed many of the Dogtown articles in SkateBoarder?
check.why: Craig Stecyk wrote and photographed many of the Dogtown pieces in the mid-1970s.

check.q: Why did SkateBoarder stop for a while in the 1960s?
choices: The first boom faded around 1965 and 1966
check.why: The magazine stopped when the first boom faded and returned in the mid-1970s.

lessons.title: Thrasher and TransWorld
lessons.mainIdea: Thrasher (1981) and TransWorld SKATEboarding (1983) carried skating through the 1980s, each with its own voice and look.
reading: By the early 1980s many skateparks had closed over insurance costs, and SkateBoarder magazine had changed direction. Skaters moved to backyard ramps, empty lots and city streets. Two new magazines followed them. *Thrasher* started in San Francisco in 1981. *TransWorld SKATEboarding* started in Southern California in 1983.

Thrasher had a rough, loud voice. It covered backyard ramps, street skating and punk bands, and its slogan, "Skate and Destroy," matched that attitude. TransWorld tended toward cleaner layouts and a slightly calmer tone, with long photo features and interviews. Skaters often argued about which one they liked better. Having both meant more photographers, writers and skaters got paid and seen.

Both magazines relied on the *sequence*, a row of photos taken a fraction of a second apart that shows a trick from start to finish. A sequence lets a reader see where the feet go at each moment, which a single photo cannot do. Thrasher later began naming a Skater of the Year, a title many skaters still treat as one of the highest honors in the sport. Many of the best-known skate photographers built their careers shooting for these two magazines.

words.d: a skateboard magazine started in San Francisco in 1981, known for a rough, loud voice
a skateboard magazine started in Southern California in 1983
a row of photos taken a fraction of a second apart that shows a trick from start to finish

look.title: When the Magazines Began
look.cite: Publication histories of the magazines; SkateBoarder's return is commonly dated to 1975
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first skate magazine and Thrasher?

check.q: Where and when did Thrasher start?
check.why: Thrasher started in San Francisco in 1981.

check.q: What does a photo sequence show that a single photo cannot?
choices: Where the feet go at each moment of a trick
check.why: A sequence is a row of photos a fraction of a second apart, so it shows a trick from start to finish.

check.q: Why did skating move toward backyards and streets in the early 1980s?
choices: Many skateparks closed over insurance costs
check.why: Many parks closed over insurance costs, so skaters found backyard ramps and streets.

lessons.title: How a Skate Photo Is Made
lessons.mainIdea: Skate photographers use wide lenses, flashes and careful timing to freeze a trick at the exact moment that shows it best.
reading: A good skate photo usually catches the peak of a trick: the highest point of an ollie, the middle of a grind, the instant a flipped board lines up under the feet. That moment lasts a tiny fraction of a second. The photographer has to know the trick well enough to press the shutter just before it, because there is always a small delay between seeing and pressing.

Many skate photographers use a *fisheye lens*, a very wide lens that bends straight lines into curves and lets the camera get close to the skater while still showing the whole obstacle. Others stand far back with a long lens to show the size of a spot. Portable *flash* units, small bright lights fired for a split second, freeze motion and light a skater who is in shadow. Photographers often place two or three flashes around a spot before the skater tries anything.

Shooting a trick can take many tries. A skater may need dozens of attempts to land it, and the photographer needs one try where the landing, the angle and the light all work. That shared work builds trust between skater and photographer. Today a phone can shoot bursts of many frames per second, so anyone can try this at a local park, as long as they stand well out of the skater's path.

words.d: a very wide camera lens that bends straight lines into curves and shows a huge area up close
a small, very bright light fired for a split second to freeze motion
the moment in a trick that shows it best, such as the highest point of an ollie

look.title: Setting Up One Shot
look.text: A photographer arrives at a low ledge in a skatepark. First, she watches the skater try the trick a few times without shooting. Next, she sets one flash on a small stand to the side, out of the skater's path. Then she kneels low with a fisheye lens about two meters from the ledge, so the ledge looks long and the skater looks tall. On each try she presses the shutter a moment before the board reaches the ledge.
look.prompt: Why does she watch a few tries before shooting, and why does she press a moment early?

check.q: What does a fisheye lens do?
choices: Makes the photo black and white
Zooms in on a skater far away
Shows a very wide area up close and bends straight lines
check.why: A fisheye lens is very wide, bending straight lines into curves while showing the whole obstacle.

check.q: Why do skate photographers often use flashes?
choices: To warn people the skater is coming
To make the board roll faster
To freeze motion and light a skater in shadow
check.why: A flash fires for a split second, which freezes motion and adds light.

check.q: Why does a photographer press the shutter just before the peak?
choices: There is a small delay between seeing and pressing
Cameras only work early in the day
The skater asks for a blurry photo
Flashes need to cool down first
check.why: Because reaction takes time, pressing a moment early catches the peak itself.

sections.title: Skate Video as an Art Form

lessons.title: The Bones Brigade on VHS
lessons.mainIdea: The Bones Brigade Video Show (1984) used home video tape to show skating in motion, and videos soon became how skaters learned and shared tricks.
reading: In 1984 Powell Peralta released The Bones Brigade Video Show, directed by Stacy Peralta. It came out on *VHS*, the home videotape format of the 1980s, so a skater could watch it on a family TV and rewind a trick again and again. Magazines could show a sequence of a few photos. A video showed the whole run, with speed, sound and timing.

Powell Peralta followed with Future Primitive in 1985 and The Search for Animal Chin in 1987. These videos mixed real skating with short scenes and jokes, and they made the Bones Brigade skaters famous far from California. Skaters copied tapes for friends, and shops played them on TVs. A teenager in a small town could now see Tony Hawk or Steve Caballero ride a ramp in real time.

Video changed how people learned. A skater could pause a tape on the frame where the back foot snapped the tail, then play it in slow motion. Some skaters say they learned their first tricks from a paused VHS tape. It also changed what a professional skater was. A pro now had to be filmed well, not just win contests, and the *video part*, a skater's own section of a video, became a major event.

words.d: the home videotape format of the 1980s and 1990s, played in a VCR
one skater's own section of a skate video, usually set to a song
a Zephyr team skater who co-founded Powell Peralta and directed its videos

look.title: Landmark Skate Videos
look.cite: Release years of the videos (Powell Peralta; Blind; Plan B)
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first Bones Brigade video and Video Days?

check.q: Who directed The Bones Brigade Video Show (1984)?
check.why: Stacy Peralta directed Powell Peralta's videos, starting with The Bones Brigade Video Show in 1984.

check.q: What could a VHS video show that a magazine sequence could not?
choices: A still frame of one moment
The whole run with speed, sound and timing
check.why: Video showed motion and sound over a whole run, not just a few frozen frames.

check.q: What is a video part?
choices: A broken piece of VHS tape
A spare part for a camcorder
One skater's own section of a skate video
check.why: A video part is a single skater's section of a video, usually set to a song.

lessons.title: Street Videos of the Early 1990s
lessons.mainIdea: Videos such as Blind's Video Days (1991) and Plan B's Questionable (1992) made street skating and the filmmaker's style central to skate culture.
reading: By the early 1990s many skaters rode city streets: curbs, ledges, benches, stairs and handrails. Video followed them. Blind's Video Days came out in 1991, directed by Spike Jonze, who later became a well-known film director. It followed a small group of skaters, including Mark Gonzales, Jason Lee and Guy Mariano, through their city. Its loose, personal style felt like hanging out with friends, and many skaters still name it among the most important skate videos.

Plan B's Questionable came out in 1992. It showed highly technical street skating, with flip tricks and long grinds done on everyday city objects. Watching it, viewers could see how far flat-ground tricks had come since Rodney Mullen's early-1980s work. Each skater's part was edited to a chosen song, so the rhythm of the music and the rhythm of the tricks matched.

These videos show skate filmmaking as an art. The filmer picks the angle, follows the skater while rolling on a board, and decides what to keep. The editor chooses the order of tricks, the song and the *ender*, the last and usually hardest trick in a part. Many famous street spots seen in these videos were private or not meant for skating, and rules there varied; skaters learning today build skills at skateparks and on small, low obstacles first.

words.d: skating on everyday city objects such as curbs, ledges and benches rather than ramps
the last trick in a video part, usually the hardest or most surprising
the person who films skating, often while rolling on a board beside the skater

look.title: Building a Video Part
look.text: An editor has forty clips of one skater and a three-minute song. First, she drops the clips that are blurry or badly framed. Next, she groups tricks by spot so the part moves from place to place. Then she places small tricks during the quiet start of the song and harder tricks as it builds. She saves the most difficult landing for the final beat: the ender.
look.prompt: Why might an editor put the hardest trick last instead of first?

check.q: Who directed Blind's Video Days (1991)?
check.why: Spike Jonze directed Video Days and later became a well-known film director.

check.q: What is an ender in a skate video?
choices: The last and usually hardest trick in a part
The first trick in a part
check.why: The ender is the closing trick of a part, usually the hardest or most surprising.

check.q: What kind of skating did Plan B's Questionable (1992) show?
check.why: Questionable featured technical flip tricks and grinds on city objects.

lessons.title: From Camcorders to the Internet
lessons.mainIdea: Better cameras in the 1990s and the internet in the 2000s moved skate video from mailed tapes to clips anyone can post.
reading: In the mid-1990s Sony released the VX1000, a digital *camcorder* (a handheld video camera). Paired with a fisheye lens, it became a standard tool for skate filmers for years. Its look, sharp and close with curved edges, is still copied on purpose today. Full-length videos moved from VHS to DVD around the early 2000s, often with extra footage and behind-the-scenes clips.

The internet changed the speed of everything. YouTube launched in 2005, and Instagram in 2010. A trick filmed in the morning could be seen around the world by night. Short clips, often under a minute, became as important as long videos. Skaters in Brazil, Japan, South Africa or Illinois could build an audience without a magazine or a company choosing them first.

Something was gained and something changed. More people can share their skating, including girls, older skaters, adaptive riders and skaters far from California, who once rarely appeared in magazines. At the same time, a constant stream of clips can make a full video part, planned and edited over a year or more, feel rare. Many skaters still treat a full part as the highest form of the art.

words.d: a handheld video camera
a short piece of video, often under a minute, shared online
a skate video with many parts, planned and edited over months or years

look.title: How Skate Video Traveled
rows: The Bones Brigade Video Show on VHS
look.cite: Release and launch years of the videos and services
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first Bones Brigade tape and the launch of YouTube?

check.q: What camera became a standard tool for skate filmers in the mid-1990s?
choices: A film camera with no lens
check.why: The Sony VX1000, a digital camcorder, paired with a fisheye lens, became standard for years.

check.q: How did YouTube (2005) and Instagram (2010) change skate video?
choices: A clip could be seen around the world within hours
They made VHS tapes the main format again
check.why: Online posting let skaters share clips worldwide quickly, without a company choosing them first.

check.q: Who gained more chances to be seen when anyone could post clips?

sections.title: Music, Zines and Doing It Yourself

lessons.title: Punk, Hip-Hop and the Soundtrack
lessons.mainIdea: Punk in the 1980s and hip-hop in the 1990s shaped skate culture, and the songs in videos and games introduced many people to that music.
reading: In the early 1980s, as skating moved to backyards and streets, many skaters listened to *punk rock*: short, fast, loud songs, often made cheaply by young bands. Punk's attitude of making things yourself, without asking permission from big companies, fit skating at that time. Some skaters played in bands, and Thrasher covered punk music alongside skating and put out compilation tapes of what it called skate rock.

In the 1990s *hip-hop* became just as important. Street skating and hip-hop both grew in cities and both treated everyday places, a plaza or a corner, as a stage. Video parts were set to rap, soul, jazz and rock, and the song a skater chose said something about who they were. A part's music could make a run feel smooth and stylish or wild and fast.

Music also carried skating to new people. When the video game Tony Hawk's Pro Skater came out in 1999, its soundtrack mixed punk and hip-hop. Many players heard those bands and rappers for the first time while playing. Today the song choice in a video part is still treated as part of the art, and filmers sometimes edit each trick to land on a beat.

words.d: short, fast, loud music, often made cheaply by young bands, popular with many 1980s skaters
a music and culture that grew in cities, including rap, DJing and dance
the music that plays with a video or game

look.title: Same Tricks, Different Song
look.text: Picture the same thirty seconds of skating played twice. The first time it runs with a fast punk song: the cuts feel quick and each landing hits like a drum. The second time it runs with a slow soul song: the same pushes and carves feel smooth and relaxed, and you notice the skater's style more than the danger.
look.prompt: How does music change what a viewer notices about a skater?

check.q: Which music did many skaters listen to in the early 1980s?
check.why: Many early-1980s skaters listened to punk, whose make-it-yourself attitude fit skating then.

check.q: What did street skating and hip-hop have in common?
choices: Both began in the 1960s on beaches
Both grew in cities and used everyday places as a stage
check.why: Both treated city places like plazas and corners as a stage.

check.q: What did the 1999 game Tony Hawk's Pro Skater do for music?
choices: Introduced many players to punk and hip-hop through its soundtrack
check.why: Its soundtrack mixed punk and hip-hop, and many players heard those artists first there.

lessons.title: Zines and DIY Culture
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters have a long habit of making things themselves: photocopied zines, backyard ramps and skater-built parks like Burnside.
reading: A *zine* (say "zeen") is a small, homemade magazine, often typed or handwritten, cut and pasted together, photocopied and stapled. In the 1980s and 1990s skaters made zines about their local crews, spots and bands, and traded or mailed them to each other. A zine needed no publisher and no advertisers. It needed a copy machine, some photos and someone who cared.

This habit is called *DIY*, short for do it yourself. When many skateparks closed in the early 1980s, skaters built wooden half-pipes and mini ramps in backyards, sometimes from plans printed in magazines. In 1990 skaters in Portland, Oregon, began pouring concrete under the Burnside Bridge without permission. The city later accepted Burnside skatepark, and it became famous around the world. In London, skaters have used the Southbank undercroft since the 1970s, and the Long Live Southbank campaign kept it open with an agreement in 2014.

DIY is a way of seeing a place and asking what it could become. It also comes with real responsibilities. Building on land you do not own can be illegal and unsafe, and good DIY projects today often work with a city or landowner, as Burnside eventually did. The same spirit drives skaters who make their own videos, photos, shirts and art, and who teach each other at the local park.

words.d: a small homemade magazine, often photocopied and stapled, made without a publisher
short for do it yourself; making things such as zines, ramps or parks without waiting for a company or city
a skatepark in Portland, Oregon, built by skaters under the Burnside Bridge starting in 1990 and later accepted by the city

look.title: Seeing What a Place Could Be
look.text: Picture a patch of bare dirt and broken concrete under a city bridge in 1990. Skaters carry in bags of cement on weekends, shape a curved wall by hand and let it dry. Over the years more walls appear. Much later, city leaders who once saw a problem start to see a public park that people travel from other countries to ride.
look.prompt: What do you think made the city change its mind about a park built without permission?

choices: A small homemade magazine, often photocopied and stapled
check.why: A zine is a homemade magazine made without a publisher, often photocopied.

choices: In a backyard pool in Santa Monica
Under the Burnside Bridge in Portland, Oregon
In a parking lot in Anaheim
check.why: Skaters began pouring concrete under the Burnside Bridge in Portland in 1990.

check.q: What does DIY stand for?
check.why: DIY means do it yourself: making things without waiting for a company or city.

review.why: Jim Phillips drew the Screaming Hand, first used in the mid-1980s.

review.q: Why did deck graphics become more important in the 1980s?
choices: Pro models let fans buy the deck of the skater they admired
Grip tape was invented in the 1990s

review.q: Put these in order from earliest to latest.
review.why: The Quarterly Skateboarder began in 1964, Thrasher in 1981 and TransWorld in 1983.

review.q: What changed when The Bones Brigade Video Show came out on VHS in 1984?
choices: Skaters could watch and rewind whole runs at home
review.why: Home video showed motion, sound and timing, and viewers could rewind tricks to study them.

review.q: Which video, directed by Spike Jonze, came out in 1991?
review.why: Blind's Video Days came out in 1991, directed by Spike Jonze.

review.q: What is the main job of a flash in skate photography?
choices: To make the photo black and white
To freeze motion and light the skater
To tell the skater when to start
review.why: A flash fires for a split second, freezing motion and adding light.

review.q: What do a zine, a backyard ramp and Burnside skatepark have in common?
choices: All were made by large companies
All were paid for by the Olympics
All came from skaters doing it themselves
